title: Australia news live: woman dies after car crashes into Melbourne restaurant; five arrested as police raid CFMEU headquarters
text:
Woman dies after a car crashes into shopping centre restaurant in Melbourne’s east
Police are investigating the death of a woman who was struck by a car that crashed into a restaurant at Westfield Knox in Wantirna South in Melbourne’s east.
Emergency services responded to reports of the crash at about 12.45pm on Monday, according to Ambulance Victoria.
The female customer, who has not yet been formally identified, died at the scene. A second customer was treated by paramedics at the scene.
The driver and passenger were both taken to Maroondah hospital in stable conditions.
Police have launched an investigation but said they “do not believe the incident was an intentional act”.
In a social media post, cafe Martini & Co said it was “temporarily closed until further notice”.
CFMEU say it’s “cooperating fully” with police after raids across several properties
The CFMEU and its staff say they are “cooperating fully” with Victoria police after five people were taken into custody during raids across six properties, including the union’s Melbourne headquarters.
Detectives from Taskforce Hawk executed search warrants on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged secret commissions and corruption in Victoria’s construction sector.
In a statement, administrator Michael Crosby said:
Criminals and bad actors in construction remain a major threat to the workers which is why we need greater regulation and scrutiny across the sector.
This administration has undertaken unprecedented reform and anyone associated with criminal elements will have absolutely no place in this union’s future.
The CFMEU said it will also launch its own internal investigations.
The scandal was a leading contributor to the ousting of former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan. The new premier, Ben Carroll, announced a royal commission last week.
James Paterson says Coalition immigration policy not finalised
The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, says the Coalition has not yet settled its immigration policy while speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing.
One of the reasons why is to do the work thoroughly and properly. Get it costed, get it modelled, consult stakeholders, so you don’t have four policies in four weeks like One Nation has had.
We’re going to take the time to get it right, so that by the time the next election comes around, Australians know exactly where we stand on migration and they can vote for or against us based on their judgment of that policy.
Asked whether he acknowledges there had also been inconsistency within the Coalition over immigration policy and migration numbers, Paterson said:
We haven’t settled our policy yet. And when we do, we will be behind it because we will have done the work to arrive at it.
We will have done the modelling, we’ll have done the costing, we’ll have done the consultation. It’ll be a rock-solid number that we stand behind.

New Zealand to introduce bill banning social media for children under 16
The New Zealand prime minister, Christopher Luxon, said on Monday his party will introduce a bill in parliament that seeks to ban children under 16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform’s global revenue for non-compliance.
The bill would require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by utilising existing account information, facial technology and digital identity documents.
“We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children,” Luxon said in a statement, adding:
Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.
It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners, the New Zealand First party, saying it would not support it.
One Nation described as ‘all over the shop’ with migration targets
Barnaby Joyce says his One Nation colleague David Farley misspoke when he said the party’s net migration target was “not too different” from Labor’s, describing it as a rookie mistake.
The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said the comments demonstrated One Nation was “all over the shop when it comes to migration”.
Farley, who won the seat of Farrer for Pauline Hanson’s rightwing party in May, ruffled feathers when he told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation’s net overseas migration (Nom) target was 130,000, it would allow an additional 100,000 migrant workers at a minimum. They would include skilled workers, backpackers, and Pacific and Timor-Leste labour through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme.
The final figure, of about 230,000, is slightly more than the Albanese’s government’s forecasts of 225,000 by 2027-28. Hanson insisted on Sunday that the party’s target was 130,000.
US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific
A US government plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration has drawn opposition from US territories in the Pacific, as the Trump administration remains locked in a race with China for control of critical ocean minerals.
On Tuesday, the Marine Mineral Administration, an agency under the US department of the interior, released a proposal to auction deep sea mining leases for 28m hectares of seafloor off the coast of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam.
The leases would allow companies to explore the seabed and potentially extract deposits of critical minerals – known as polymetallic nodules – that could be used in batteries, electronics and defence technologies. Many environmental groups have opposed deep sea mining, arguing that more research is needed on its effects on marine ecosystems.
Other projects ‘more needed and urgent’ than Suburban Rail Loop, Victorian premier suggests
Continuing on from the previous post …
In an interview on ABC Radio Melbourne, host Raf Epstein pressed the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, on whether the two tunnel-boring machines in the ground in Burwood, about to begin tunnelling to Glen Waverley next month, will proceed.
Carrollreplied:
The expectation is yes. The boring machines are there. There is a contract in place and that work will go ahead. But I am also having a very good look at how we fix up potholes, get on with Airport Rail, get on with Melton electrification. There are other projects that are so much more needed and urgent, and I want to make sure that Victorians know I’m governing for every corner of this state and every region of this state too.
Asked whether he will sign the contracts to build the SRL East underground train stations before the election, Carroll said he’ll have “more to say on this in the very near future”.
Epstein:
I interpret that as 100% you’re not going to build the stations. You’re delaying building the stations. Is that the right interpretation?
Carroll:
An orbital line is needed for our state, but we need to do it where it’s the best value for taxpayers … I’m not here to make any announcements on that except to say I’m having a very good look at this project, as I am all projects, to make sure we’re getting value for money. And I’ll have more to say later this week.
Victorian premier teases update on Suburban Rail Loop
The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, did the rounds on Melbourne radio this morning, suggesting he will soon provide an update on the future of the Suburban Rail Loop.
When Carroll became premier just under a month ago, he said he would be ordering a review into the costly 90km public transport project, which would also consider whether billions of dollars worth of already-signed construction contracts could be redirected.
The state government has signed about $14.5bn worth of contracts for the first stage of the loop, known as SRL East – a 26km stretch of tunnels between Cheltenham and Box Hill.
Asked by 3AW’s Tom Elliot whether he wanted to push ahead with the project, Carroll replied:
What Victorians want is a relentless focus on the basics: health, education, community safety. They do not want to be the government to be doing big, expensive projects.
They want to focus on the little things that matter so much to them. Now, on the Suburban Rail Loop, I will have more to say very soon. What I can say is … the era of ripping up contracts is over. I will stick to contracts that have been signed.
Having said that, though, Tom, I will work with the people building Suburban Rail Loop to get better value for taxpayers.The Suburban Rail Loop, an orbital line, makes sense, but it cannot be crowding out everything else we need to do as a government. Airport Rail, Melton electrification, filling potholes and doing the job properly – these are the things Victorian want from their leader and their government.
Albanese maintains there will be ‘no change’ to WA’s share of GST while he is PM
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is speaking in Perth, where he said there will be “no change” to WA’s share of the GST while he is in the top job:
What I believe is very clearly there will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements while I’m prime minister. That is my view.
That has consistently been my view. The floor of 75% will absolutely stay. I think that WA deserves that. Because WA contributes to the national economy, and helps to drive that economy.
The WA premier, Roger Cook, said West Australians would be “relieved and pleased to hear the words from the prime minister today that Western Australia’s arrangements for the GST will remain”.
Cook said:
You don’t come to Western Australia on 45 occasions without appreciating that the Western Australian economy is driving the national economy. And we are very pleased that the prime minister has backed WA.
Five arrested as police raid CFMEU headquarters in Melbourne
Nino Bucci
Five people have been taken into custody after Victoria police investigating allegedunion corruption raided properties including the headquarters of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) on Monday.
Police said in a statement:
Detectives from Taskforce Hawk executed warrants at six addresses this morning as part of a current investigation into information provided re secret commissions.
One of the warrants was executed at a premises on Elizabeth Street in Melbourne. Five people have been taken into custody and are being interviewed by police.
Further information will be provided later this afternoon.
The Elizabeth Street property is the headquarters of the Cfmeu. Taskforce Hawk was established to investigate allegations of corruption in the construction sector after revelations of allegedgraft involving the CFMEU on Victoria’s so-called Big Build.
The scandal was a leading contributor to the ousting of former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan. The new premier, Ben Carroll, announced a royal commission last week.
AFL CEO says ‘actions of a few’ don’t define football industry amid Swans scandal
Luca Ittimani
The AFL CEO, Andrew Dillon, won’t say the game has a culture problem, saying the actions of a few Sydney Swans players don’t define the industry, after an incident that led to an allegation of sexual assault currently being investigated by Victorian police.
Separately, five Swans players have been stood down for the rest of the season for breaching club standards by “drinking … staying out late … and bringing women back to the hotel”. No one has been arrested or charged in relation to the investigation and the Guardian understands the players deny criminal wrongdoing.
Speaking to reporters in Melbourne just now, Dillon was asked if the AFL had a cultural problem. He said:
I think the actions of a few don’t define the actions of the entire industry.
He also said the league also won’t investigate the Sydney Swans incident, including hair testing for illicit substance use, until the police have finished investigating.
The players have reportedly denied using illegal drugs. Dillon said the club’s penalties were adequate and brought “accountability”.
Look, we saw an amazing crowd for the AFLW game, the highest crowd that the Sydney AFLW has had, over 16,000, and then we had a crowd of over 30,000 for the men’s game. There was some people that left the games in between, but that’s happened in other double headers. It was a special day for the Swans. It was a tough day.
